text: We came at nine before the school arrived and it was empty and cool and the terrace at the top is flat with a view of the whole city. My four year old managed the side ramp at the back with me holding the rail, which is the only way I would attempt it.

Beautiful nave and the cliff walkway is level once you are in. The seventy steps up from the road are the problem and the terrace toilets are the other problem. Take a taxi up and bring your own expectations about the last fifty metres.

Flat stone, benches along the wall, and the whole crowd facing inland to photograph the city rather than the sunset in front of them, which is the joke. The path from here to Mount Mary is the smoothest walking surface in Bandra.
We pushed a pram right onto the terrace with no trouble and the kids could run on flat stone without me chasing them. Busy at seven and it gets worse by half past, so come at six.

A kilometre of buildings on one side and nothing on the other, with laundry on the balconies and a working courtyard. We walked right down the middle and nobody objected. My daughter asked why we could not live in the courtyard and I had no good answer.
Flat, level, and shaded which is more than most of this area offers, and there is a colonnade to sit in when it rains. No public toilet anywhere near, which is the only thing I would change.
Everyone photographs the hotel from the promenade and about four people a week walk onto the open ground behind it. Flat, empty, no shade, and the best half hour of quiet I had in Bandra. Take a hat.

Wide open and completely exposed, so at eleven in the morning with a two year old this was too hot and too bright. Come at seven and it is lovely. There is nothing to hide behind if the weather turns.

Level from the gate, a lawn, a graveyard under trees, and the only church in Bandra with a working toilet. We sat under the trees for an hour in January and it was ten degrees cooler than the road. The painted ceiling is worth looking up for.
Calm and shaded and nobody minds, but it is a working church on a working week, so there is a service or a rehearsal or a locked gate for much of it. Sunday morning is the reliable window.

We walked it at eleven in the morning when there is no traffic, the rail line is below us, and the flyover gives shade the whole length. Gentle gradient, good surface, pram fine. The sea appears on the west side and then disappears again.

I walked it at six on a weekday by mistake and it is a car park. The road is impassable and the pavements are gone. The description says to avoid rush hour and it means seven and eleven, not just those exact minutes.

The bread is the reason. We went at six when the queue starts and got felfeli hot from the oven. Sweets are absurdly cheap by weight and the children ate their weight in them. Pavement is level on the main stretch.

Busy and the pavement narrows to about three feet once the queue is out, and every shop has a step up from the pavement. The food is worth it. Sit at a table inside rather than browse if your knees are bad.

Packed by ten and the pavement is a strip. Bought chillies and a plant, both good, both cheap. With a stroller it was a moving crowd and I would not do it again, but walking it alone it is a good Sunday.
Got there at eight and had the lane to ourselves for twenty minutes. Vegetables, flowers, a food section at the end. Gone by one, so do not plan an afternoon around it.

Steep stone road up and mostly foundations, but the two vaults and the cannon earn the climb, and there is a view over the village from the top. We were there at eight and had it to ourselves. No shade once the sun is up.
The description says a steep approach and I read that as inconvenient. It is a climb. We turned round a third of the way up in the heat with no water and no shade between us and the bottom.
Genuinely cheap second-hand stuff and you can walk the whole street on level ground. On a Sunday it is a solid crush though, and that is a problem for anybody who finds crowds difficult.
We went on a Tuesday morning, early, and it was manageable, and we walked it at a slow pace. The stalls vary hugely and the good ones are spread out. No toilets, which is the thing to plan for.

Left at half five, at the landing before the light, and watched the boats come in. Nobody performed anything for us. The family cooked what landed and we ate it sitting on the sand. Booked two weeks out and I would book earlier.

The description is honest about the ground, and I still took a five year old onto sand, mud and rock at six in the morning with no toilet. It was not a good call and the morning was long. Lovely for adults, wrong for a small child.
signalTags: not for a five year old

text: The photographs of the lines overhead are worth the walk and the colour is extraordinary. The ground is wet, there are open drains, and it smells. Twenty minutes, then leave. I would not bring anyone who is not walking deliberately.

Went anyway despite knowing better, because the photographs look good. Wet broken ground, open drains, a dhobi shouting at us to move. Ten minutes and we left and I felt like a tourist who had gone somewhere she was not welcome.

Ninety minutes in a working studio with tea while the painter explained one canvas. No obligation to buy and no pressure of any kind, which is what I wanted. A narrow stair with a turn, so not for a wheelchair.
Pleasant and informative and about half the time is conversation you could have in a cafe. The work is the point and there is no shop, so if you wanted to buy something, wrong address.

Two and a half hours at the wheel, hands ruined, and we left with nothing because the piece is fired in three weeks. They posted a photograph of it in the glaze and it is now on our wall. Book a week out and do not plan anything afterwards.

Two and a half hours standing at a wheel with no chance to sit, and my back gave up at the ninety minute mark. The description is accurate and I did not read it. Fine for a fit twenty five year old, wrong for me.

Requested a Goan forty five they clearly loved and the whole room reacted. Twenty people, one turntable, a steep short stair, and by midnight the sound system was genuinely too much. Go at ten rather than midnight.
A steep stair, a low ceiling, a sound system at full volume and forty people my age would not enjoy. I managed the stair. My wife did not enjoy the rest and we left at half eleven.

Sold by weight off a glass counter, so my children chose their own and then asked for more. Clean, bright, six tables, and a proper lozenge for very little money. Step-free from the pavement and no queue after seven.
Six of us and the queue was fifteen minutes and the six tables were all taken, so we stood at the counter like everyone else. The sweets were worth it. Come with two people rather than six.

Five of us, one long lunch, and the fish curry was genuinely good rather than an afterthought. The room is loud and the family run it themselves, so nothing is rushed and nothing is explained. One flight of stairs with a turn, then level.

Excellent food and a narrow stair with a turn, which defeated us, so we did not eat. They offered to bring the food down and we took them up on it, which is a kind thing and meant a plastic table in the kitchen. Good people.

Took a one year old and it was the first restaurant in five days that did not stress us out. Step-free, real high chairs, a change of space, and a menu with something plain for a child who will not eat anything brown. Expensive and worth it.
The food is ordinary for the price and the play corner is a television in a corner. It is priced as a family-friendly place rather than a good restaurant, which is honest. Noisy at one o clock.

Twelve murals across six quiet lanes and my nine year old was the one pointing at them. The lanes are flat and calm which is the surprise on that side of Bandra. Three of the twelve had already been repainted since the map was made.
The lanes are flat and quiet, which was our whole brief, and we had to turn back twice because of steps between lanes that the route does not mention. Two of the murals are now shops.
signalTags: route is not step by step

text: You look down on trains going both ways and the whole skyline is in front of you. Better than I expected. Unpaved and uneven in a couple of places, so I would not bring a stroller, and there is nothing to buy and no toilet at all.
I carried our two year old for most of it because of the unpaving, and the sunset was better on the photographs. Lovely idea, wrong for a small child on that ground.

A preserved 1950s foyer with the original ticket window and staircase, and my eleven year old thought it was the coolest forty five minutes of the trip. Volunteers open it, so it took an email four days earlier and a donation, and it was worth the trouble.
I walked past on the day and there was a sign saying closed and no way to know when it was open. Do not build a plan around it, and check by message a few days before.

Standing in a village lane at five waiting for a bell that took four minutes to arrive, and then the whole lane went quiet. Free, nothing to book, and it made the place feel like a place. Five minutes, not forty.
We got there at half six, the bell had gone, and there was nothing to see. The description says five in the evening and means five, not six and a half.

A mechanical tracker organ with no microphone, which means the sound arrives from somewhere rather than from everywhere. Seventy minutes in a stone church with good acoustics. Free seat at the back if you get there before the service.
I brought an eight year old to an organ recital, which was optimistic. The acoustic is loud and reverberant and she covered her ears. Lovely for us, wrong for her.

Two hundred people and about four hundred kites on a flat fenced field, with a making tent so nobody is disappointed. Toilets on site, which at a field event is the thing you look for first. It is the single best two hours we had in Bandra with three children.

Wind, noise, four hundred strings at head height and no shade on the field. My wife lasted forty minutes. The description does say fenced, which is accurate, and I did not read that it meant no shelter at all.

Out into the harbour while the auction was happening alongside us, then back along the coast. Life jackets, a crew of two, and the sea state checked before we left. Wet, loud, and two hours that felt like forty minutes.

A stone step down to a moving deck and no way to make it safe for a six year old, so we did not go. That is the right decision and it cost us the morning, and they refunded without argument, which I appreciated.
Sixty rupees, a steel kettle, and a bench along the wall that nobody minds you using for twenty minutes with a paper. I have had this four mornings running. Cash only.
Good chai and the bench has a back, which I appreciated, and there is nowhere to sit if the bench is taken. Pavement is noisy and there is no toilet. The tea is worth the stop.

Two hours twenty including the film and the interval, and it took the whole afternoon. The lift reaches the balcony, the foyer is the best part, and the food court is better than a cinema food court has any right to be. Step-free the whole way.
I have ninety minutes and this needs a hundred and fifty plus a queue. I rejected it on the number alone, which is the correct use of a duration field. Went and had a sandwich instead.

It rained hard all week and this was the only thing that saved two of our days. Permanent roof, wide aisles, level floor, and toilets inside, which almost no market in this city has. Flowers, cloth, dry provisions, and a hardware stall. Not exciting and completely reliable.

Flat, dry, and there is a lift to a mezzanine, which is unusual. It is also a working market rather than a place to spend an hour, so we did forty minutes and moved on. Toilets were the deciding factor for us.

Flat stone, twenty people, and nobody minds if you sit on the wall at the back instead of stretching on a hard surface, which is what my husband did for the whole hour. Finished exactly at sunset. No toilets, so go beforehand.
Arrived late and joined at the front, which is a bit exposed. Otherwise cheerful and informal and nobody performed the relaxation bit at anybody. Free.

Order at the counter, take the plate to the table, play carrom for two hours. They taught me carrom in ten minutes without being condescending about it. Loud, social, and step-free. No toilets, which is a real gap for a two hour visit.

Four parts, unamplified, in a stone room, with the practice door propped open. Free, no collection, and we left before it finished so as not to disturb. Goan polyphony in the building it was written for is not something you can get anywhere else in the city.

I have hearing loss and there is no microphone to lose and no loop, so I heard a noise rather than singing. The people beside me were moved. Wrong for us and nobody there had any way of knowing I was there.

Shaded, flat, benches with backs, and nobody to buy anything from. We took a flask and sat for an hour. The kiosk was shut and I am glad we had planned for that. No toilets, so it is short and sweet rather than a whole morning.
Good flat space under the trees and a six year old could run about, but there is a slope down to the water that I did not notice until we were on it. Stay on the upper level.

Somebody spoke for two minutes before the music started and explained what we were about to watch, and that converted both of my children from fidgeting to interested. Flat, metal chairs, and a hard stop at seventy minutes, which is right for that age.
Good performance of a small set, and the hall is bare with a hard floor, so it is not a comfortable ninety minutes of seating. Booked it, would book it again, would not bring a very long day to it.

All the shops have the same brass at the same price and there is no bargaining, so it is a buying trip rather than a browsing one. Air-conditioned, which is why I went. The cafe next door is the better half.
Bought a brass thing for a gift and haggled in my head for a while before remembering there is no haggling here. My son was bored. Fine if you know what you want and where you are going.

A junction that is a car park at eight and a bar street at eleven. Six of us, a table on the roof of one, and food from the stalls downstairs. Loud, crowded and the best night we had in Bandra, but you will not enjoy it if crowds or kerbs are a problem for you.

Kerbs, a shoulder-to-shoulder crowd and stairs into every one of the bars. I could not get off the pavement. My son enjoyed it enormously and I stood at the edge for an hour. The description should be blunter about the crowd.
